questions.q: Distinguish between the trabeate and arcuate styles of construction.
answer: Medieval Indian architecture used two main techniques of construction.

answer.text: In the trabeate or 'post-and-lintel' style, used between about the eighth and thirteenth centuries, roofs, doors and windows were made by laying a horizontal beam across two upright columns. Temples, mosques, tanks and palaces of this period were built this way.
From the late twelfth century the arcuate style spread, in which the weight of the roof was carried by arches, and the 'true' arch and the dome appeared.
The change was helped by high-quality limestone cement and superior mortar, which made it possible to build strong arches and domes.

questions.q: Why did rulers build temples, mosques and other structures?
answer: Rulers invested heavily in building for reasons that went beyond mere shelter.

answer.text: Grand temples and mosques displayed a ruler's devotion to god and were meant to be models of the world, the cosmos in miniature. Building them proclaimed the ruler's power and religious merit.
Constructing wells, tanks and reservoirs — such as Iltutmish's Hauz-i-Sultani — showed the ruler as a caring provider, and won him praise and gratitude.
Because temples were centres of wealth, devotion and authority, they were also symbols of a kingdom's strength, which is why victorious rulers sometimes attacked the temples of those they defeated.

questions.q: Describe the development of temple architecture in medieval India.

answer.text: Between the eighth and thirteenth centuries, kings built magnificent temples both as places of worship and as displays of their power and devotion. Temples grew ever taller and more richly carved.

The Kandariya Mahadeva temple at Khajuraho, built by the Chandelas, and the Rajarajeshvara, or Brihadeshwara, temple at Thanjavur, built by the Chola king Rajaraja, are outstanding examples. The latter had the tallest tower of its time.

A temple had a sanctum, the garbhagriha, housing the deity, over which rose a tall tower, the shikhara or vimana. Around it were halls, gateways and finely sculptured walls showing gods, dancers and scenes of life.

answer: Thus medieval temple architecture reached great heights of size and artistry, glorifying both the gods and the kings who built them.

questions.q: How did the buildings of the Delhi Sultans and the Mughals reflect their power and ideas?

answer.text: The Sultans and Mughals introduced the arch and the dome, built on the arcuate technique, along with tall minarets and spacious mosques, tombs and forts. The Qutb Minar and the great congregational mosques are early examples.

The Mughals raised splendid forts, palaces, mosques and garden-tombs. Humayun's Tomb, Akbar's Fatehpur Sikri and Shah Jahan's Taj Mahal and Red Fort show the height of their art, using marble, sandstone, inlay work and formal charbagh gardens.
Such buildings advertised the wealth, taste and authority of the rulers, linked them to earlier traditions, and served as centres of religion and government.

answer: Thus the grand buildings of the Sultans and Mughals were both practical structures and powerful symbols of imperial glory.

questions.q: Why did rulers build large monuments, temples and public works?

answer.text: Rulers built grand temples, mosques and tombs to display their wealth, power and devotion. A magnificent structure announced the greatness of the king and won him fame and the blessings of the divine.
By building temples or mosques and endowing them, rulers earned religious merit and the goodwill of priests and people. Such acts helped justify their rule as righteous.

Rulers also constructed useful public works, such as tanks, wells, canals, roads and rest houses for travellers. These served the people, aided trade and farming, and further increased the ruler's reputation for care and generosity.

answer: Thus rulers built to proclaim their power, earn religious merit and serve the public, all of which strengthened their authority.
